judgment.rationale: Both SFIs sit in Grade 3 (rank 3) READING AND PHONICS. The second SFI is Term 1, Sub-strand Phonics: 'Recognises that some sounds are represented by a number of different spelling choices (play, pain, plate; feet, read, key; ...)'. The first SFI is Term 3, Sub-strand Paired/Independent Reading: 'Reads aloud to a partner'. Direction is earlier Term 1 to later Term 3, which is permitted within one grade. Substantively, secure recognition of alternative grapheme-phoneme spelling patterns underpins accurate, fluent decoding of connected text, which is what oral reading to a partner in the paired reading slot requires; the Term 3 activity applies the Term 1 phonic knowledge in independent, sustained reading with an audience. This is a decoding-to-applied-fluency support relationship, not mere wording overlap (the nomination's token/trigram overlap was only the trivial token 'a' and trigrams 'rea', 'ead', 's a', and the shared Grade 3 ancestor alone carries no semantic weight). Confidence is moderate because the supporting relationship is inferred from skill content rather than explicit CAPS cross-reference, and source evidence for both endpoints is truncated (24 omitted source-evidence items each); the first endpoint's LC evidence is also truncated.

The Term 4 statement is not mere repetition: its LCs ('Suggests topics for discussion', 'Asks questions for information', 'Reports back on the group's work') add learner-initiated topic selection, purposeful information-seeking questioning, and oral reporting of group work, a substantive extension in independence and complexity beyond the Term 3 ask/answer exchange. Earlier-to-later term within one grade is a permitted developmental direction, and competence in asking and answering questions in discussion plausibly supports success in the more autonomous Term 4 discussion role. Evidence is bounded: both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each) and the first endpoint's LC evidence is truncated, but the available statement text and LCs are consistent and non-contradictory.

Fluency in encoding and forming words from learnt letter sounds plausibly supports success in producing multiple correct, legible sentences, so the permitted lower-to-higher-grade direction (second_to_first) is supported; the differing sub-strands (Shared/Independent Writing versus Handwriting) make this a supportive rather than strict prerequisite link, hence moderate confidence. Shared tokens alone ('writes', 'writing') were not treated as sufficient evidence. However, the texts are distinct bullets with different foci (exploratory reasoning across subjects vs. supported story prediction from title/cover cues), with no evidence that one is a broadened or deepened version of the other, and both sit at the same grade rank and same Term, so no developmental direction is substantively supported. Token/trigram overlap is low (jaccard ~0.13) and driven by function words ('and','e','g','to') plus 'think', which alone is not progression evidence. judgment.rationale: Both SFIs sit in Grade R, Term 2 (same coordinate rank 0, shared Term ancestor), so same-term direction is permitted if substantively justified. The first (Listening and Speaking (Oral), 'Daily activities' sub-strand) has learners sing songs, recite rhymes and perform actions with the whole class, building an oral repertoire of familiar songs and rhymes (LCs: 'Recites rhymes with the whole class', 'Sings songs with the whole class'). The second (Emergent Reading, Phonological/Phonemic Awareness) requires identifying rhyming words in 'well known rhymes and songs' (e.g. Humpty Dumpty) — it explicitly presupposes familiarity with that same repertoire and moves from performing/reproducing to analysing sound patterns within it. Oral fluency with the rhymes therefore supports success in the phonological-awareness task; the direction is not reversed, since rhyme detection is the more analytic, reading-oriented capability. Shared tokens ('rhymes','songs') are corroborated by this pair-specific content link, not relied on alone. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated (24 omitted items each), which limits but does not contradict this reading.

judgment.rationale: Both Skills sit in the same Grade 3 (rank 3), Term 3, WRITING skill area, but under different printed Sub-strands: 'Handwriting' (copying written text from board/textbooks/work cards with correct letter formation and spacing in joined/cursive script) and 'Shared, Group and Independent Writing' (writing and illustrating sentences on a topic to contribute to a class library book). The LCs confirm distinct capabilities: transcription/copying accuracy versus composing and illustrating own sentences for an audience. They are coherent, mutually reinforcing components of the same term's writing programme, taught in parallel, but the evidence shows no substantive expansion or dependency that would justify a same-rank, same-Term developmental direction either way; copying a model text does not establish composition capability and composing does not presuppose cursive copying. Decided on text, Sub-strand and coordinate evidence only; shared ancestors, same source page and generic token overlap ('and', 'the', 'to') were not treated as semantic support. Both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each), so the bounded excerpts may not show all printed detail.

judgment.rationale: Both Skills sit in Grade R (rank 0), Term 4, Skill Area 'Emergent Writing', but in different sub-strands: 'Works with words' (identifies a letter or a space between words in print, e.g. in names, familiar words or a book - a print-concepts/letter-awareness skill) and 'Emergent Handwriting' (forms some lower case letters correctly, starting and ending in the correct place - a motor letter-formation skill). They cohere substantively around the same unit of print, the letter, and are taught together in the same Term 4 Emergent Writing table (page 56), so they reinforce each other as complementary recognition and production skills. The evidence does not, however, show one as a staged expansion or capability extension of the other: nomination signals are shared ancestry, same-term source-page proximity, weak lexical/trigram overlap and a generic shared LC tag set ('emergent', 'letter', 'writing'), and with identical Grade and Term rank there is no substantive basis for asserting a developmental direction either way. relatesTo is therefore the supported judgment rather than buildsTowards.

judgment.rationale: Both Skills sit in Grade R, Term 1, Skill Area 'Emergent Reading' (same coordinate rank 0, same term), but under different printed sub-strands: 'Recognises own name and names of at least five other children in the class' under 'Begins to make meaning of written text', and 'Matches words to words on objects and named items such as name cards on tables, door, window' under 'Emergent reading skills'. They are substantively coherent complementary print/word-recognition work: LC tags 'name recognition / sight words / written text' versus 'word matching / labels / print awareness', both anchored to name cards and classroom print. Within the same grade and same term, the evidence does not establish which capability is the more complex or dependent one — perceptual word-to-word matching and independent name recognition reinforce each other rather than showing a documented expansion in scope, length, or independence — so a directional buildsTowards is not warranted. Shared ancestors, page proximity (both page index 37, same table row 4) and weak token overlap ('and', 'name') are nomination signals only, but the shared emergent-reading name/print content supplies genuine pair-specific coherence. Note both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted evidence items each) and all nodes carry upstream audit/merge context, which limits but does not contradict this reading.

judgment.rationale: Both SFIs are Grade 2 Skills in the Reading and Phonics / Daily Phonic Activities sub-strand, tagged 'phonics'. The second SFI sits in Term 1 (revising common consonant digraphs sh, ch, th at word endings, e.g. fi-sh, ri-ch, clo-th) and the first sits in Term 4 (revising the 'silent e'/split digraph pattern, e.g. cake, time, hope). This is an earlier-Term to later-Term direction within the same grade, which is the only permitted developmental orientation here. Secure recognition that two letters can work together as a single sound unit within a word (consonant digraphs) plausibly supports success with the more abstract split digraph, where a vowel and a final 'e' are separated by a consonant and must be read as one vowel pattern; the Term 4 statement extends the digraph concept from adjacent consonant pairs to discontinuous vowel patterns rather than merely repeating it. Shared tokens ('revises', 'words', 'digraph') and the shared Grade 2 ancestor alone would not justify an edge, but the pair-specific content extension does. Note that both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted evidence items each), so the judgment rests on the printed bullet text, identity scopes and Learning Components supplied.

judgment.rationale: Both SFIs sit under Grade 3 (rank 3) but in different skill areas and terms: the first is 'Reads own writing to the class' (Term 3, WRITING > Shared, Group and Independent Writing), the second is 'Reads enlarged texts such as poems, big books, posters and electronic texts as a whole class with the teacher (shared reading)' (Term 1, READING AND PHONICS > Shared Reading). Within Grade 3 only Term 1 -> Term 3 (second_to_first) would be a permitted developmental direction, but the evidence does not show that teacher-led whole-class shared reading of enlarged published texts is a capability on which reading one's own composed writing aloud to the class depends; the latter's demand is authorship and sharing of own text, not decoding enlarged texts. There is nevertheless genuine, pair-specific coherence beyond the shared tokens 'class'/'reads': both are whole-class oral reading experiences that develop audience awareness and fluency in reading connected text aloud, linking the reading and writing strands. That supports symmetric relatesTo rather than a developmental edge. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated and both carry upstream merge/audit context, so a stronger dependency claim is not warranted.

judgment.rationale: Both SFIs are Grade 3 WRITING > 'Shared, Group and Independent Writing' bullets about sentence-level grammar in written work: Term 1 'Uses present, past and future tense correctly' and Term 4 'Uses conjunctions to form compound sentences'. Their LCs share the tags 'grammar' and 'writing', giving substantive conceptual coherence as complementary written-language conventions. However, the two address distinct grammatical features (verb tense accuracy versus clause-joining with conjunctions); the later statement is not an expansion, deepening, or increased-complexity version of the earlier one, and correct tense use is not evidenced as supporting compound-sentence construction beyond generic co-membership in Grade 3 writing grammar. The only other linkage signals are a shared Grade 3 ancestor, same-grade rank (gap 0), and low lexical overlap driven by the word 'uses', which alone does not establish a developmental dependency. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated (24 omitted items each) and all ancestors carry upstream merge/audit context, so no stronger directional claim is made; symmetric relatesTo is recorded with canonical endpoint order preserved.

judgment.rationale: Both Skills sit under Grade R (rank 0), but the source evidence places the second SFI in Term 1 / Emergent Reading / 'Emergent reading skills' ('Uses memory skills to recall items seen such as letters, shapes or concrete objects') and the first SFI in Term 4 / Emergent Writing / 'Emergent Writing:' ('Makes attempts at familiar forms of writing, using known letters. For example, "writes" a letter home'). Direction is therefore constrained to earlier Term 1 to later Term 4 (second_to_first), which is also the semantically supported direction: visual memory for recalling seen letters and shapes (LC tags 'memory', 'recall', 'visual memory') underpins the later, more complex capability of reproducing known letters independently in a purposeful, familiar written form (LC tags 'known letters', 'familiar forms'). This is a substantive extension from recognition/recall of letter forms to productive use of those letters in writing, not mere repeated wording; the only lexical overlap is the token 'letters', so the judgment rests on the term/skill-area evidence and skill content rather than surface similarity. Both endpoints' source evidence is truncated, which limits detail but does not contradict this reading.
